media.author: Nesnad

questions.description: The green hair gel for every slice of Quark bread.
questions.question: This herb is green, hollow like a straw and tastes of onion. Chopped into tiny rings, it goes on Quark bread. Which herb is it?
hints: It's related to onions and garlic.
It's best cut with scissors.
Its German name, “Schnittlauch”, means “cutting leek”.
questions.fun_fact: You can eat the purple flowers of chives too.

media.credit: Voxbyrox · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Voxbyrox

questions.description: A schnitzel that has never been a schnitzel in its whole life.
questions.question: I'm a cooked German sausage. In eastern Germany, I'm cut in thick slices, breaded, fried and served with pasta and tomato sauce. What am I?
hints: In the East, the dish is still called a “schnitzel”.
It was a classic in East German school cafeterias.
The dish is named after a man with a rifle and a hat in the forest.
questions.fun_fact: Order a “Jägerschnitzel” in the East and you often get breaded sausage; in the West, it's a schnitzel with mushroom sauce.

media.credit: Renee Comet (Photographer) · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Renee Comet (Photographer)

questions.description: The reward at the end of the hike that makes every uphill step worth it.
questions.question: You stop at an inn in the Black Forest for a “Vesper”. What usually ends up on the table?
questions.answer: Bread, cured ham, sausage and cheese
hints: It's a cold meal.
People like to eat it off a wooden board.
In Bavaria, the same thing is called “Brotzeit”.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Vesper” comes from the Latin “vespera”, which means “evening”.

media.credit: pictures Jettcom · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: pictures Jettcom

questions.description: Sausages have been sizzling here for longer than some castles have been standing.
questions.question: The “Historische Wurstkuchl” by the Stone Bridge in Regensburg is said to be one of the world's oldest cookshops. How far back does its history go?
hints: “One of the oldest in the world” is meant seriously.
It started as a kitchen for the workers on a building site.
The Stone Bridge was built in the High Middle Ages.
questions.fun_fact: Regensburg's Stone Bridge is one of the oldest stone bridges still standing in Germany.

media.credit: Jakub Hałun · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jakub Hałun

questions.description: A salad where the vegetables only get a supporting role.
questions.question: Fleischwurst cut into strips, pickles and lots of mayonnaise: what is this salad from the deli counter called?
hints: It's a classic on a Brötchen.
It's more white than green.
Its name leaves out the sausage and uses a broader word instead.
questions.fun_fact: Germany's official food guidelines, the Deutsches Lebensmittelbuch, set how much meat has to be in a Fleischsalat.

media.credit: A.Savin · FAL · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: A.Savin

questions.description: A traveler, a well and a tree: that's all a catchy tune has needed for almost 200 years.
questions.question: In the folk song “Am Brunnen vor dem Tore”, a tree like the one in the photo stands by the well. What kind of tree is it?
hints: People like to make tea from its blossoms for colds.
Its leaves are heart-shaped.
A famous grand boulevard in Berlin is called “Unter den …”.
questions.fun_fact: The words were written by the Dessau poet Wilhelm Müller; Franz Schubert set them to music in 1827 in his song cycle “Winterreise”.

media.credit: JiriMatejicek · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JiriMatejicek

questions.description: A song starring a little bedbug, and yet nothing itches.
questions.question: The song goes “Auf der Mauer, auf der Lauer sitzt 'ne kleine Wanze.” What do you do when you sit “auf der Lauer”?
hints: Cats love doing it in front of a mouse hole.
You stay very quiet while doing it.
You watch closely without being seen yourself.
questions.fun_fact: With every verse you leave one more letter off “Wanze” and “tanzen”, until in the end almost only humming is left.

media.credit: Jebulon · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jebulon

questions.description: A song where your closet gives away who you're in love with.
questions.question: In the children's song “Grün, grün, grün sind alle meine Kleider” (green are all my clothes), you wear green because of your sweetheart's job. What is the sweetheart?
hints: He spends a lot of time in the forest.
He often wears a hat with a feather.
He sits up in a raised wooden stand, watching for deer.
questions.fun_fact: In other verses you wear black, for example, because your sweetheart is a chimney sweep.

media.credit: Joe Ross from Lansing, Michigan · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Joe Ross from Lansing, Michigan

questions.description: A lullaby for kids who want to squeeze in some math before falling asleep.
questions.question: At bedtime, children hear the song “Weißt du, wie viel Sternlein stehen” (do you know how many little stars there are). Who, the song says, counted all the stars?
hints: The song says not a single star is missing from his great count.
The song says he also knows every child.
You talk to him in your evening prayers.
questions.fun_fact: The words were written by the pastor Wilhelm Hey and first printed in 1837.

media.credit: Chad Ajamian · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chad Ajamian

questions.description: Dirndl, yodeling, a never-ending smile: the must-see show for every Saturday night in front of the TV.
questions.question: As a child she won the Grand Prix der Volksmusik with her father, comes from the Vogtland and was married to Stefan Mross. Who?
hints: She grew up in Saxony.
Her father Eberhard is a folk music singer too.
Her first name is very close to her ex-husband's.
questions.fun_fact: Her winning song from 1992 was called “Über jedes Bacherl geht a Brückerl”.

media.credit: user:UlrichAAB · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: user:UlrichAAB

questions.description: Germany's loudest party spot isn't actually in Germany at all.
questions.question: Where does the “Ballermann” on Mallorca get its name from?
hints: The name is really a Spanish word that Germans said their own way.
There are lots of them along the Playa de Palma, all numbered.
It means “Balneario 6”, a small beach stand.
questions.fun_fact: “Balneario” means something like “bathing place” in Spanish, and German vacationers turned it into “Ballermann”.

media.credit: Ivan Curra · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ivan Curra

questions.description: A reformer in bronze who has stood on the same spot forever and still refuses to take anything back.
questions.question: In which year was the great Luther Monument in Worms unveiled?
hints: By then, Luther himself had been dead for more than 300 years.
The monument was paid for with donations from all over Germany.
The year is in the 19th century.
questions.fun_fact: Besides Luther, the Worms monument shows other figures such as Jan Hus, and it is one of the largest Reformation monuments in the world.

media.credit: Immanuel Giel · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Immanuel Giel

questions.description: Probably the most famous wall where scribbling was officially allowed.
questions.question: In what year did artists from around the world paint the East Side Gallery in Berlin?
hints: Before that, painting on this spot was strictly forbidden.
It happened shortly after the Berlin Wall fell.
Germany was reunified in the same year.
questions.fun_fact: At more than 1.3 km (0.8 mi), the East Side Gallery is the longest surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: The capital has wet feet, and not just when it rains.
questions.question: Which river flows right through the middle of Berlin?
hints: Tour boats on it cruise past the Reichstag.
It flows into the Havel in Berlin's Spandau district.
It also flows through a forest region famous for its pickles.
questions.fun_fact: The Spree is actually longer than the Havel, the river it flows into at Spandau.

media.credit: Chris j wood · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chris j wood

questions.description: A dialect is speaking up for itself here, so please don't laugh.
questions.question: I show surprise with “Ei verbibbsch!”, say “nu” when I mean yes, and turn Kaffee into “Gaffee”. Which dialect am I?
hints: In polls about favorite dialects, I often end up near the bottom.
My home is in eastern Germany.
You can hear me in Leipzig and Dresden.
questions.fun_fact: For his Bible translation, Martin Luther drew on the Saxon chancery language, which back then was considered especially refined.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: France is right next door, and some things just stuck around in Saarland.
questions.question: It’s named after a French city, it’s a classic in Saarland and it’s often eaten in slices. What is a “Lyoner”?
hints: You buy it at the butcher’s counter.
In Saarland, people also fry it in a pan with potatoes.
Elsewhere it’s often called Fleischwurst.
questions.fun_fact: In Lyon itself, the sausage is hardly known by this name, and where it really comes from is still unclear.

media.credit: Pascal Dihé · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pascal Dihé

questions.description: Dresden, the Elbe, Baroque style and a church with quite an eventful life story.
questions.question: You’re standing in front of Dresden’s Frauenkirche. What was on this spot for about 50 years before it was rebuilt?
hints: Nothing new was built on this spot in East German times.
The church was destroyed in February 1945.
Many of the old stones were used again when it was rebuilt.
questions.fun_fact: The dark stones in the light-colored walls come from the old church, which makes it look like a jigsaw puzzle.

media.credit: Matthias Frank · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Matthias Frank

questions.description: A furry resident of the capital who never had to go apartment hunting.
questions.question: The bear on Berlin's coat of arms: how many legs is it standing on?
hints: It is black and sticks out its red tongue.
It looks ready for a fight, with its claws stretched forward.
It stands upright, like a person.
questions.fun_fact: The top prize of the Berlin Film Festival is a bear too: the Golden Bear.

media.credit: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de

questions.description: There's so much Baltic Sea air here, they should really start exporting it.
questions.question: How many other German states does Mecklenburg-Vorpommern border?
hints: To the north lies the Baltic Sea, to the east Poland.
To the west it borders Schleswig-Holstein and Lower Saxony.
To the south, only Brandenburg is left.
questions.fun_fact: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern has about 2,000 lakes, including the Müritz, the largest lake that lies entirely within Germany.

media.credit: Siarhei Besarab · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Siarhei Besarab

questions.description: A tower that tells you the time, if you can just count the lights fast enough.
questions.question: The Rheinturm is about 240 m (787 ft) tall, stands next to the state parliament and shows the time with lights. In which city is it?
hints: People here prefer Altbier to Kölsch.
The Königsallee is a famous shopping street here.
This city is the state capital of North Rhine-Westphalia.
questions.fun_fact: The lights on the tower's shaft are said to form the world's largest decimal clock.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: A pastry with its arms crossed and a different name depending on where you are.
questions.question: Who would typically call this pastry a “Brezn”?
hints: People there often call a bread roll a “Semmel”.
The region is in the south of Germany and reaches the Alps.
It’s the state whose capital is Munich.
questions.fun_fact: You can spot a Swabian pretzel by its thin little arms and its fat “belly”.

media.credit: Tamorlan · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tamorlan

questions.description: It hangs out all day and still has a bad reputation.
questions.question: Bats were once seen as witches’ animals that get tangled in your hair at night. Bats are mammals. What are their wings made of?
hints: Birds and bats fly in very different ways.
The wings are soft and stretchy and fold up like an umbrella.
The wing is a rebuilt hand, and you have its material all over your body too.
questions.fun_fact: Bats don’t get caught in hair: thanks to echolocation, they can even dodge thin threads.

media.credit: W.carter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: W.carter

questions.description: A broom, a cauldron and a grumpy witch’s cat cooked up this saying together.
questions.question: What do Germans mean when they say “Das ist wie verhext!”?
wrong_answers: Someone is acting like a witch
Something has gone suddenly, eerily quiet
hints: People usually say it when they’re annoyed.
It feels as if someone had put a curse on things.
The key won’t fit, the printer won’t print, the puzzle piece is missing.
questions.fun_fact: In the old days, people really did blame witches when the milk went sour or the butter wouldn’t set.

media.credit: InfosReseaux · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: InfosReseaux

questions.description: A wolf who clearly bit off more than he could chew at dinner.
questions.question: In the Brothers Grimm fairy tale, the big bad wolf eats Little Red Riding Hood and her grandmother. Who gets them both out of his belly?
hints: He hears the wolf snoring loudly.
He spends a lot of time in the forest.
He carries a rifle and wears a green hat.
questions.fun_fact: Afterwards they fill the wolf's belly with heavy stones.

media.credit: F R · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: F R

questions.description: A dance floor the lawn laid out all by itself.
questions.question: Sometimes mushrooms grow in a perfect circle on a meadow. According to legend, when did elves dance there?
hints: Elves don't like being watched by humans.
Elves love soft, silvery light.
The stars are shining in the sky then.
questions.fun_fact: The mushroom ring forms because the fungus's web of threads underground grows a bit further outward every year.

media.credit: User:Mrs skippy · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: User:Mrs skippy

questions.description: A pinch of panic for the kitchen table.
questions.question: Superstition says that if you spill salt, you should quickly throw a pinch of it. Where?
hints: The salt is meant to hit someone lurking behind you.
That someone is the devil.
He sits on the side where your heart beats.
questions.fun_fact: In Leonardo da Vinci’s “The Last Supper,” Judas has knocked over a salt cellar.

media.credit: Jorge Royan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Royan

questions.description: The magic word after a big “Achoo!”
questions.question: In Germany, someone sneezes and you wish them not to get sick. Which word do you call out?
hints: You say it right after the sneeze.
Lots of Americans say it too.
It's the German word for “health.”
questions.fun_fact: People once believed that a sneeze could let illness or evil spirits slip into the body.

media.credit: Captain MarcusL · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Captain MarcusL

questions.description: A wish machine standing in every meadow.
questions.question: It's white and fluffy, and you blow it away and make a wish. What hangs from each of its tiny parachutes?
hints: The wind carries the tiny parachutes far away.
Where they land, something happens later.
A new dandelion grows from it.
questions.fun_fact: The tiny parachutes of a dandelion puff, the “Pusteblume”, can be carried many kilometers by the wind.

media.credit: Monstieur Kraken · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Monstieur Kraken

questions.description: A bird that has to fill in for somebody else entirely.
questions.question: In old German curses like “Zum Kuckuck!” or “Weiß der Kuckuck!”, the cuckoo stands for someone people didn't want to name. Who?
hints: People feared that saying his name would summon him.
He is said to have horns and a horse's hoof.
He supposedly lives in hell.
questions.fun_fact: German folk belief says you should jingle the coins in your purse when you hear the first cuckoo call in spring, so your money won't run out all year.

media.credit: Tisha Mukherjee · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tisha Mukherjee

questions.description: The farmers' weather report always had a good eye for color.
questions.question: What does the old German farmers' saying „Grüne Weihnachten, weiße Ostern“ (“green Christmas, white Easter”) predict?
questions.answer: No snow at Christmas, but snow at Easter
wrong_answers: Snow at Christmas, but lots of sun at Easter
Lots of rain in December, lots of sun at Easter
Green fir trees at Christmas, white Easter eggs
hints: It's about the weather on two holidays.
The two holidays sort of swap their looks.
White is what drifts down from the sky in winter.
questions.fun_fact: In much of Germany there's usually no snow at Christmas, so a “green Christmas” is more the rule than the exception.

media.credit: smunster · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: smunster

questions.description: Under the Christmas tree, a shoebox looks more harmless than it really is.
questions.question: According to superstition, you should never give anyone shoes. What will the person do with them otherwise?
hints: Shoes are made for walking, after all.
The shoes carry them in one particular direction.
In the end, the giver is left alone.
questions.fun_fact: As a remedy, the person getting the shoes often hands over a small coin, so the shoes count as bought.

media.credit: No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: High ceilings, creaky floorboards and a landlord who calls it “charm”.
questions.question: Ceiling decorations like the one in the photo are typical of German Altbau apartments. What are they usually made of?
hints: The material is white and is mixed with water.
It is worked while soft and then hardens.
Doctors use it for hard casts on broken bones.
questions.fun_fact: Many old buildings in German cities date from the Gründerzeit boom around 1900, and their ceilings are often over 3 m (10 ft) high.

media.credit: Globetrotter19 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Globetrotter19

questions.description: Every five years, a town in northern Hesse becomes the center of the world.
questions.question: Since 1955, documenta has been held in Kassel for 100 days, about every five years. What is it?
hints: You walk through halls, parks and museums there.
Joseph Beuys had 7,000 oak trees planted for it.
It is also called the “museum of 100 days.”
questions.fun_fact: For Beuys's work “7000 Oaks,” trees were planted across Kassel from 1982, each next to a basalt column, and the last one went into the ground in 1987.

media.credit: Harmish Khambhaita · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Harmish Khambhaita

questions.description: Probably the most-framed pair of hands in Germany.
questions.question: Prints of Albrecht Dürer's “Praying Hands” hang in many living rooms. In what year was the drawing made?
hints: Dürer lived in Nuremberg during the Renaissance.
A few years earlier, Columbus had reached America.
In the same year, Michelangelo began painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
questions.fun_fact: The hands were a study for an altarpiece whose central panel was lost in a fire in 1729, but the drawing survived.

media.credit: Fred Romero from Paris, France · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fred Romero from Paris, France

questions.description: Here the gables have more swirls than a wedding cake.
questions.question: Grand buildings in Hameln, Lemgo and Hämelschenburg Castle, built around 1520 to 1620: what is this architectural style called?
hints: The style was influenced by Italy and the Netherlands.
Typical features are decorated gables and bay windows, locally called “Utluchten”.
It is named after the river that Hameln lies on.
questions.fun_fact: A famous example is the Rat Catcher's House in Hameln, where an old inscription recalls the legend of the Pied Piper.

media.credit: Bernd Schwabe in Hannover · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernd Schwabe in Hannover

questions.description: A hundred meters, a blink of an eye, and in the end a belly flop trimmed in gold.
questions.question: “I sprint for Germany, threw myself across the finish line in Munich in 2022 and became European 100-meter champion.” Who am I?
hints: I come from Westphalia.
At the 2024 Olympics, I won bronze with the relay team.
My last name starts with “Lücken…”.
questions.fun_fact: Lückenkemper fell as she dived across the finish line, but she still got there first.

media.credit: Eckhard Pecher (Arcimboldo) · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eckhard Pecher (Arcimboldo)

questions.description: Others retire; she'd rather do one more lap on the ice.
questions.question: Claudia Pechstein competed at her eighth Olympic Games in Beijing in 2022. In what year were her first?
hints: Back then, the Summer and Winter Games were still held in the same year.
The Games took place in Albertville, France.
They were the first Winter Games of reunified Germany.
questions.fun_fact: At Beijing 2022, Pechstein, at nearly 50, carried the German flag at the opening ceremony.

media.credit: Arne Müseler · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arne Müseler

questions.description: A whole swimming pool full of gold, and nobody had to dive for it.
questions.question: Kristin Otto, later a presenter on German TV channel ZDF, swam for East Germany at the 1988 Seoul Olympics. How many gold medals did she win there?
hints: No other woman won more at those Games.
At the time, it was a record for a woman at a single Olympics.
It was half a dozen.
questions.fun_fact: Otto won her gold medals in three different strokes: freestyle, backstroke and butterfly.

media.credit: Arne Müseler · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arne Müseler

questions.description: It roars louder here than at a lawnmower race.
questions.question: This racetrack in Baden-Württemberg, near Mannheim, is named after its town and has often hosted Formula 1. Which one?
hints: The town is close to Heidelberg.
Part of its grandstands is called the “Motodrom”.
The name starts with “Hocken…”.
questions.fun_fact: Until 2001, the track ran deep into the forest; in 2002 it was made much shorter.

media.credit: Morio · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Morio

questions.description: The thing that helps more than any excuse after you fall off your bike.
questions.question: I'm small, I stick to scraped knees, and I have a soft pad in the middle. Which brand name do many people know me by?
hints: I belong in every first aid kit.
My name starts like the old trading league of Hamburg and Lübeck.
Hanse + Pflaster (German for “bandage”) almost makes my name.
questions.fun_fact: Hansaplast, Nivea and Tesa all come from the same Hamburg company: Beiersdorf.

media.credit: Saimmx · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Saimmx

questions.description: A slogan that makes every piggy bank squeal with joy.
questions.question: An electronics store ad on TV uses the slogan “Geiz ist geil!”. Which decade are you most likely in?
hints: The Deutsche Mark was already gone by then.
The campaign ran while the euro was still brand new.
It started in 2002.
questions.fun_fact: The Jung von Matt agency came up with the slogan for the Saturn chain, and it ran until about 2007.

media.credit: Intel Free Press · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Intel Free Press

questions.description: A lifesaver for anyone who misspells a word in the middle of a school dictation.
questions.question: It has two ends: one makes blue fountain pen ink disappear, the other writes over it. What is this pen called in Germany?
hints: It's in almost every pencil case in German primary school.
It goes with the fountain pen the way an eraser goes with a pencil.
Its name sounds like it finishes off the ink.
questions.fun_fact: The erasing end bleaches the blue dye chemically, which is why it usually doesn't work on black ink.

media.author: Petar Milošević

questions.description: Even people with GPS get lost in here.
questions.question: In Ravensburger's “Labyrinth” you hunt for treasures, and when you set up, one path tile is always left over. What is it used for?
hints: It looks just like the other path tiles and passes from player to player.
You use it on every turn, before you move your piece.
Afterwards, a whole row slides along by one space.
questions.fun_fact: The game was invented by Max Kobbert and came out from Ravensburger in 1986.

media.credit: Joseolgon · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Joseolgon

questions.description: If you want to become German champion, you have to keep collecting, just like with a sticker album.

hints: A draw gets you less.
A draw is worth exactly one point.
It's the number of sides of a triangle.
questions.fun_fact: Until 1995, a win in the Bundesliga was worth only two points.

media.author: ticketsluxury

questions.description: The most expensive piece of paper in many fans' wallets.
questions.question: A Bundesliga season ticket covers every home game of the season. How many Bundesliga home games is that?
hints: There are 18 teams in the Bundesliga.
Each team plays every opponent once at home and once away.
It is exactly half of 34.
questions.fun_fact: At some clubs, fans spend many years on a waiting list for a season ticket.

media.author: Lewis Clarke

questions.description: A coin that gets around more than any backpacker.
questions.question: In the circle game „Taler, Taler, du musst wandern“, an old silver coin travels around. Which modern currency is named after it?

In Dutch, “Taler” became “daalder”.
It's what people pay with in the USA.
questions.fun_fact: The name Taler comes from the “Joachimsthaler”, a silver coin from the town of Joachimsthal in Bohemia.

media.author: Unknown / Commissioned by Ulrich, Duke of Württemberg

questions.description: A crime under the palm trees, and the loot is rock hard.
questions.question: In the children's song “Wer hat die Kokosnuss geklaut?” (“Who stole the coconut?”), which animals shout it together as a whole gang?
hints: These animals love to climb.
At the zoo, their house often has lots of climbing ropes.
They swing from branch to branch and like bananas.
questions.fun_fact: Botanically, a coconut isn't a nut at all but a drupe, a fruit with a stone inside.

media.credit: Ivar Leidus · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ivar Leidus

questions.description: If you have no scissors on you, just grab a sword.
questions.question: In the song “Sankt Martin ritt durch Schnee und Wind”, Martin cuts his cloak with his sword. Into how many pieces?
hints: The song is sung at the lantern parades in November.
A freezing beggar sits in the snow, and Martin gives him some of his cloak.
One piece for Martin, one piece for the beggar.
questions.fun_fact: The word “chapel” (German “Kapelle”) comes from Martin's cloak (Latin “cappa”), later kept as a relic in a small prayer room.

media.credit: PAUL FARMER · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PAUL FARMER

questions.description: Ten little fellows who can never sit still. Sound familiar?
questions.question: They wiggle back and forth, crawl up and down, and hide at the end. What are the “Zehn kleine Zappelmänner” (ten little wiggle men)?
hints: You play it with small children, without any toys.

The study of coats of arms is named after him.

Mosquitoes had few places left to breed, and a disease known today from the tropics went away.

Its name sounds like the German word for the peel of a fruit.

To flood old brown coal pits

The water is moved across the European watershed.

The city is famous for Oktoberfest.

The country of Georgia is there.

The Tsar's army was still far away at the time.

questions.question: Anselm Kiefer, born in Donaueschingen in 1945, likes to work with straw, ash and lead. Where did he buy tons of old lead from?
hints: The material had been exposed to the weather for decades.
It came from a very famous building.
The building has two huge towers and stands on the Rhine.
questions.fun_fact: Kiefer has lived in France since the 1990s and turned an old silk factory in Barjac into a huge art estate.

hints: The word describes what happens to the stain.
After wiping, you can't see the stain anymore.
In German, it's the opposite of “da”.
questions.fun_fact: The name Zewa comes from the pulp factory Zellstofffabrik Waldhof: ZE-llstoff WA-ldhof.

questions.question: Miracoli comes in a box with tomato sauce and a spice mix. What kind of dish is it?
hints: You need a big pot of water to make it.
The name sounds Italian.
The classic box holds long, thin spaghetti.
questions.fun_fact: Miracoli has been sold in Germany since 1961.

questions.description: A school-bag classic that plenty of parents once wrote with too.
questions.question: Lamy from Heidelberg makes the “safari”, which many schoolchildren learn to write with. What kind of writing tool is it?
hints: You need one from elementary school on.
You refill it instead of sharpening it.
You put ink cartridges into it.
questions.fun_fact: The Lamy safari has been around since 1980, and it was designed especially for young people.

questions.description: Some salads fill you up, others just cause trouble.
questions.question: Audio dramas used to come on cassette. What had happened when you got “Bandsalat”?
wrong_answers: The tape had played to the end
The player was running too fast
hints: Despite the name, nothing here gets eaten.
In a salad, everything gets tossed and mixed up.
A pencil often helped fix the problem.
questions.fun_fact: For Bandsalat, a pencil came to the rescue: you stuck it into the cassette and carefully wound the tape back in.

questions.description: High above Berlin shines someone who is definitely not afraid of heights.
questions.question: This golden figure stands high up on a column in Berlin. Who does it show?
hints: The column was built after wars that were won.
The figure comes from the myths of the ancient Greeks and Romans.
The figure is called Victoria.
questions.fun_fact: The figure is over 8 m (27 ft) tall, and Berliners lovingly call her “Goldelse” (Golden Elsie).

questions.description: An apple doesn't fall far from the tree, but somewhere its pronunciation takes a big leap.
questions.question: North of this dialect line, Germans say “Appel” for apple; south of it, “Apfel”. What is it called?
hints: It separates Central German from Upper German.
It's named after a town in Rhineland-Palatinate.
The town is famous for its huge Romanesque imperial cathedral.
questions.fun_fact: The dialect lines in the Rhineland run so close together that linguists call them the “Rhenish fan”.

questions.description: Knights, dragon slayers and castle ladies, talking long before anyone fixed the spelling rules.
questions.question: The medieval German Nibelungenlied begins: “Uns ist in alten mæren wunders vil geseit.” What does “mæren” mean?
hints: Many Middle High German words sound almost like modern ones, but mean something else.
The first line tells the audience what they're about to hear.
Think of the German word “Märchen”.
questions.fun_fact: The German word “Märchen” (fairy tale) is a diminutive of “Mär” and first meant “little tale”.

questions.description: In Cologne, even the beer barrel has a first name.
questions.question: In Cologne, a small 10-liter (2.6-gallon) keg of Kölsch is called a “Pittermännchen”. Which first name is hidden in it?
hints: It's a name from the Bible.
A famous apostle had this name.
The biggest bell of Cologne Cathedral also carries this name in Kölsch: “Decke Pitter”.
questions.fun_fact: Kölsch is traditionally served in narrow 0.2-liter (about 7 oz) glasses called “Stangen”.

questions.description: One man, piles of questionnaires, and sentences all of Germany had to translate into its own dialect.
questions.question: From 1876, Georg Wenker had schools translate whole sentences into their dialect. In which city is the “Deutscher Sprachatlas” still based?
hints: The city lies on a tributary of the Rhine.
Its university was founded in 1527 as the first Protestant university.
It is home to St. Elizabeth's Church, one of the oldest Gothic churches in Germany.
questions.fun_fact: Wenker's questionnaires went to tens of thousands of school towns; one sentence reads: “In winter the dry leaves fly around through the air.”

questions.description: A math problem from Rhöndorf, no calculator needed.
questions.question: Konrad Adenauer was born in 1876 and became Chancellor in 1949. How old was he when he took office?
hints: Before that, he was mayor of Cologne from 1917 to 1933.
Count from 1876 to 1949.
Up to 1900 is already 24 years, then add 49 more.
questions.fun_fact: Adenauer stayed in office until 1963 and was 87 when he stepped down, older than any other German chancellor.

questions.description: In the East, more wanted than any report card.
questions.question: Western chocolate is to candy as Western jeans are to …?
hints: You find them in the closet, not in the fridge.
You need them every morning after you get up.
You put them on.
questions.fun_fact: East Germany sewed its own jeans, for example the “Wisent” brand, but Western jeans sent in family packages were far more wanted.

questions.question: From 1963 on, what was the Stasi prison on the Kaßberg in Karl-Marx-Stadt mainly used for?
questions.answer: as a transit stop to the West
wrong_answers: as a prison for young people
as a school for Stasi officers
as a warehouse for seized parcels
hints: Most prisoners stayed here only a short time.
At the end, a bus was waiting, headed for Giessen.
West Germany paid a lot of money for each of them.
questions.fun_fact: From 1963 to 1989, West Germany bought the freedom of more than 33,000 political prisoners from East Germany.

questions.description: A word everyone in the mountains understands and everyone on the plains takes for a typo.
questions.question: The Höllentalferner lies on the north side of the Zugspitze. What does the Alpine word “Ferner” mean?
hints: The word is used mainly in Bavaria and Tyrol.
It lies high up in a shady bowl below the summit.
On the Zugspitze plateau, a Ferner is partly covered with big tarps in summer.
questions.fun_fact: The Southern Schneeferner has melted so much that it no longer counts as a glacier.

questions.description: Eastern Bavaria has its own wall, and nobody had to build it.
questions.question: The rock wall called the Pfahl runs a long way through the Bavarian Forest. What is it made of, almost entirely?
hints: The Bavarian Forest is ancient bedrock, not a former seabed.
A pocket knife leaves no scratch on this mineral.
Rock crystals are made of exactly this mineral.
questions.fun_fact: The Pfahl stretches about 150 kilometers (93 miles) across eastern Bavaria.

questions.description: A principle that sounds more boring than it is, and matters more than you'd think.
questions.question: Even the government must obey the law, courts are independent, and anyone can defend themselves in court. What is such a state called?
hints: Germany's Basic Law (Grundgesetz) makes this principle part of the constitution.
Nobody is above the law, no matter how powerful.
In German, its name shares a word with “Rechtsanwalt” (lawyer).
questions.fun_fact: Under the Basic Law's “eternity clause”, the rule-of-law principle is one of the rules that can never be abolished.

People in the host country speak a Romance language.
The opening ceremony took place on the Seine.
questions.fun_fact: In 2024, Paris hosted the Summer Olympics for the third time, after 1900 and 1924.

questions.description: A jersey that looks like it was meant for a totally different party.
questions.question: Manuel Neuer is a goalkeeper, so he wears a different jersey from his teammates. How many players per team wear a goalkeeper jersey on the field?
hints: The goalkeeper usually stands at the very back, in front of the goal.
Only the goalkeeper may play the ball with their hands inside their own penalty area.
The other ten players all wear the same jersey.
questions.fun_fact: The goalkeeper's colors must be different from all the other players' and from the referee's too.

It has no keys and no sliders.
Singers stand right in front of it, often with a pop filter in between.

On those days, the river rose all the way up to that spot.

My opposite is the end.

You run and jump with them.

Jeeps and binoculars in the savanna are typical of it.

Popcorn goes well with them.

You smell with it.
